message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how to launch a Google Compute Engine VM with an **NVIDIA RTX A6000** GPU running **Ubuntu 20.04 LTS**.  
I’ll give you:

| What you’ll see | Why it matters |
|-----------------|----------------|
| `gcloud` CLI command | Quick, scriptable, works from your terminal |
| REST‑API (curl + JSON) | Useful if you’re calling the API directly from code |
| Required pre‑steps | Make sure you can actually run the command |

---

## 1️⃣ Pre‑conditions

| Step | Command / Action | Notes |
|------|------------------|-------|
| Enable the Compute Engine API | `gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com` | Needed once per project |
| Enable the GPU API | `gcloud services enable accelerator.googleapis.com` | Needed once per project |
| Create a service account key (if you’ll use the REST API) | `gcloud iam service-accounts keys create key.json --iam-account <YOUR_SA>@<PROJECT_ID>.iam.gserviceaccount.com` | Keep the key safe – it’s your credentials |
| Install the NVIDIA driver on the image | The image we’ll use already contains the driver, but you can also add a startup script to install newer drivers if needed |

> **Tip:** Replace `<YOUR_PROJECT>` and `<YOUR_ZONE>` with your own values.

---

## 2️⃣ gcloud CLI – One‑liner

```bash
gcloud compute instances create rtx-a6000-demo \
    --project=<YOUR_PROJECT> \
    --zone=us-central1-a \
    --machine-type=n1-standard-8 \
    --subnet=default \
    --network-tier=PREMIUM \
    --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE \
    --provisioning-model=STANDARD \
    --accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-a6000,count=1 \
    --boot-disk-size=50GB \
    --boot-disk-type=pd-balanced \
    --image-family=ubuntu-2004-lts \
    --image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud \
    --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh \
    --tags=http-server,https-server \
    --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
```

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type=n1-standard-8` | 8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM – enough headroom for GPU workloads |
| `--accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-a6000,count=1` | Adds one RTX A6000 GPU |
| `--boot-disk-size=50GB` | Size of the OS disk |
| `--image-family=ubuntu-2004-lts` & `--image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud` | Pulls the latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh` | Optional: runs a shell script at first boot (e.g., to install CUDA, cuDNN, or other libraries) |
| `--tags=http-server,https-server` | Opens ports 80/443 if you plan to host a web app |
| `--scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform` | Full access – adjust scopes if you want least‑privilege |

> **Note:** You can change the zone (`us-central1-a`) to any zone that supports GPUs (check [GPU availability](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus#available_zones)).

---

## 3️⃣ REST API – cURL + JSON

If you prefer to call the API directly (e.g., from a CI/CD pipeline), here’s a minimal example.  
Assume you have a service account key (`key.json`) and you’ve set the environment variable `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` to point to it.

```bash
# 1. Get an OAuth 2.0 access token
TOKEN=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)

# 2. Build the JSON payload
cat <<EOF > payload.json
{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-demo",
  "machineType": "zones/us-central1-a/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "diskSizeGb": 50,
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/<YOUR_PROJECT>/zones/us-central1-a/types/nvidia-tesla-a6000"
    }
  ],
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "<YOUR_SA>@<YOUR_PROJECT>.iam.gserviceaccount.com",
      "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\napt-get update\napt-get install -y cuda-toolkit-11-7"
      }
    ]
  },
  "tags": {
    "items": ["http-server","https-server"]
  }
}
EOF

# 3. POST the request
curl -X POST \
  "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/<YOUR_PROJECT>/zones/us-central1-a/instances" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @payload.json
```

### Key points

* **Endpoint**: `https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/{project}/zones/{zone}/instances`
* **Authentication**: OAuth 2.0 bearer token (obtained via `gcloud auth application-default print-access-token`)
* **JSON fields**:
  * `machineType`: full resource path (`zones/.../machineTypes/...`)
  * `guestAccelerators`: list of GPUs (`nvidia-tesla-a6000` is the correct type)
  * `disks.initializeParams.sourceImage`: uses the image family for Ubuntu 20.04 LTS
  * `metadata.items[0].value`: optional startup script (here installing CUDA 11.7)

> **Security tip:** Never hard‑code the access token in scripts. Use `gcloud auth application-default print-access-token` or a service account key that’s rotated regularly.

---

## 4️⃣ After creation

Once the instance is running:

1. SSH into it: `gcloud compute ssh rtx-a6000-demo --zone=us-central1-a`
2. Verify the GPU: `nvidia-smi`
3. Install any additional software (CUDA, cuDNN, PyTorch, TensorFlow, etc.) as needed.

---

## 5️⃣ Wrap‑up checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✔️ | Compute Engine API enabled |
| ✔️ | GPU API enabled |
| ✔️ | Correct zone selected |
| ✔️ | Machine type has enough CPU/RAM |
| ✔️ | GPU type matches your hardware (RTX A6000 → `nvidia-tesla-a6000`) |
| ✔️ | Image family set to `ubuntu-2004-lts` |
| ✔️ | Proper scopes / IAM roles granted |
| ✔️ | Optional startup script installed (for CUDA, cuDNN, etc.) |

That’s all you need! Run the `gcloud` command or the REST snippet, and you’ll have a fully‑functional Ubuntu 20.04 VM with an RTX A6000 GPU ready for deep‑learning, rendering, or any GPU‑heavy workload. Happy computing!
